meta.title: Corvus ECMA-262 regex engines: the Industry benchmarks
meta.lede: Every Corvus ECMA-262 regex engine, its platform's own regex engines and V8, over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance. Every engine ran on this runner in this hour, in one job, so a figure compares across languages as well as within one.
facts: GitHub-hosted ubuntu24 20261018.339.1, AMD EPYC 9V45 96-Core Processor, 4 cores
meta.method:
Where the figures come from. This repository's nightly workflow runs each engine repository's published container image, at its latest release, one after another in one job on one runner; each image runs its engines, its platform's competitors and V8 over the workloads, then the ECMA-262 test data for compliance. So the figures of every engine run here were measured on one machine in one hour.

Compliance beside an engine's name is its result on the ECMA-262 test data, whose answers are V8's: the share of the data it answered as V8 does, right over everything judged (the counts are in its tooltip), "the oracle" for V8, and "not ECMA-262" for an engine that implements another dialect, whose figures are a reference for speed and not for answers.

V8 appears once, from the .NET run; the V8 figures of the C, C++, Fortran, PHP, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, Swift runs are not shown.

.NET

From the image of corvus-dotnet/Corvus.Regex.Ecma262 (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-dotnet:1.0.1), run here at 10f727f.

Each figure is one Count over the whole text: every match found, as the benchmark of dotnet/performance measures it. The Corvus rows run under the u flag, which .NET has no mode for; counts agree on 53 of the 57 rows, and the four apart are $ and . at CRLF, where ECMA-262 counts CR as a line terminator, and \w, which .NET takes as Unicode letters and digits.

Where this library is slower, and why. Four kinds of row read above 1.0, each the price of an ECMA-262 rule .NET does not apply: . and $ at CRLF, where ECMA-262's . stops at CR as well as LF, so .* finds 36,491 matches to .NET's 26,105 at parity per match; case-insensitive patterns under the u flag, whose search must find the long s and the Kelvin sign as forms of s and k, which .NET's search ignores; a class that admits a supplementary character (two units) before a literal at a fixed distance, so the distance is not fixed ([a-q][^u-z]{13}x); and non-ASCII literals over UTF-8, where every Cyrillic or Chinese character is two or three bytes with no rare byte among them, against UTF-16's one rare unit per character. The other rows above 1.0 are within a few percent of parity and read either side of it from run to run.

The engines are .NET's interpreter (RegexOptions.None), .NET's source generator ([GeneratedRegex]), this library's interpreter over UTF-16, this library's source generator over UTF-16 and over UTF-8, and V8 (Node 24's RegExp, the oracle of the test data) over the same texts with the same flags as the Corvus rows, its matches counted by a test loop that advances lastIndex as matchAll does. The UTF-8 rows match the same text as bytes, with nothing transcoded.

The bar is the mean of BenchmarkDotNet's default job (one launch, warm-ups and iterations as it settles them, fifteen or more) and the whisker one standard deviation of its iterations; a row's ratio is read against its neighbours' rather than to the last few percent. Allocated is the bytes the benchmark allocated per operation; the library allocates nothing per match once its working memory has grown.

The host is a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner, by the daily benchmarks workflow: every engine in one job on one runner, so the figures of a run are comparable with each other; nothing is pinned, so a run is not comparable with the pinned record to the last few percent. .NET 10. Commit 10f727f, 2026-10-21T19:30:59Z.

Rust

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-rs (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-rs:v0.1.1), run here at 2c42dfe.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, after an empty match going on one character later. This crate and regress run with the workload's flags and u, regex with the pattern as it is and the flags i, m and s, V8 with gu added.

C

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-rs (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-c:v0.1.1), run here at 2c42dfe.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, after an empty match going on one character later. The C library and QuickJS's libregexp run with the workload's flags and u (libregexp over the text as QuickJS holds a string: 8-bit when every character is Latin-1, UTF-16 otherwise), PCRE2 with its JIT and the pattern as it is in UTF mode with the flags i, m and s, V8 with gu added.

C++

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-cpp (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-cpp:v0.1.1), run here at 18ceda8.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, after an empty match going on one character later. The C++ library runs with the workload's flags and u, its global search made once per text and walked as a range; std::regex (ECMAScript) and Boost.Regex (its ECMAScript syntax, with ^, $ and . read as ECMA-262 reads them) over the UTF-8 bytes, SRELL over the text as UTF-8, each with the workload's flags; RE2 with the pattern as it is and the flags i, m and s; V8 with gu added.

Python

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-py (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-py:v0.1.1), run here at 4c2e05c.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, with finditer, after an empty match going on one character later. This package runs with the workload's flags and u, over the text as a str and as UTF-8 bytes; Python's re and the regex package with the pattern as it is and the flags i, m and s; V8 with gu added.

Ruby

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-ruby (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-ruby:v0.1.1), run here at e164c12.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, after an empty match going on one character later. This gem runs with the workload's flags and u, over the text as a UTF-8 String and as a UTF-16LE String, each match taken as a Match with each_match; Ruby's Regexp (Onigmo) with the pattern as it is and the flags i and s (as Ruby's m), each match taken with String#scan; V8 with gu added.

PHP

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-php (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-php:0.1.1), run here at 2b45027.

Each figure is one count of the matches a global search finds over the whole text, after an empty match going on one character later. This extension runs with the workload's flags and u, over the text as a string and as Utf16 text, with Regex::countMatches; PHP's PCRE functions with the pattern as it is, the flags i, m and s and UTF mode, with preg_match_all; V8 with gu added.

Swift

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-swift (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-swift:v0.1.1), run here at 568d859.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, as a Swift program counts them. This package runs with the workload's flags and u, over the text as a String (UTF-8) and as [UInt16], with matchCount; Foundation's NSRegularExpression (ICU), with numberOfMatches, and Swift's Regex, counting matches(of:), with the pattern as it is and the flags i, m and s; V8 with gu added.

R

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-r (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-r:v0.1.1), run here at ead872c.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, as an R program counts them. This package runs with the workload's flags and u, with ecma_count over the pattern compiled once; base R's gregexpr with perl = TRUE (PCRE2) and without (TRE, which has no m or s flag), and stringi's stri_count_regex (ICU), each given the pattern in each call as R programs use them, with the pattern as it is and the flags i, m and s; V8 with gu added.

Fortran

From the image of corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-fortran (ghcr.io/corvus-dotnet/corvus-regex-ecma262-fortran:v0.1.1), run here at aabff0a.

Each figure is one count of every match a global search finds over the whole text, as a Fortran program counts them. This binding runs with the workload's flags and u, over the text as a character variable (UTF-8) and as an integer(int16) array (UTF-16), with regex_t%count; glibc's POSIX regex (regcomp and regexec, extended syntax, through ISO_C_BINDING) with REG_ICASE for i and REG_NEWLINE for m, and fortran-regex (a port of tiny-regex-c), each searching on after every match; V8 with gu added.
